subject: Social Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: What Makes a Market? Needs, Wants, and the Hampi Bazaar
periods.visual_aids: Projected or printed image of the Hampi Bazaar / Virupaksha temple street

time_bands.activity: Students examine the image of the Hampi Bazaar and, individually, write down three things they notice and one question the image raises for them. The teacher then asks two or three students to share their question, without answering yet, to build curiosity about what made this market thrive.

The teacher reads aloud the two Portuguese traveller accounts — Domingos Paes calling Hampi 'the best-provided city in the world' and Fernao Nuniz describing craftsmen producing golden jewellery, rubies, and pearls in the streets — and asks: What goods are mentioned? Who are the buyers and sellers? What does this tell us about how markets connect people and goods across distances? Students annotate their paper with answers.

Students distinguish needs from wants using the Hampi evidence: they sort the goods named in the accounts (grains, silk, precious stones, animals) into a two-column table labelled Needs and Wants, then defend one placement in writing — explaining why they placed a good in its column. The class briefly compares choices, surfacing the idea that the same good can shift category depending on context.

The teacher closes by asking: Beyond selling things, what else did the Hampi Bazaar do? Students contribute orally — connecting people, traditions, ideas — and the teacher records their words as a shared definition of 'market' on the board, noting that markets can be physical or online, and are known as bazaar, haat, or mārukatté in different regions.

periods.section_context: Hampi Bazaar, Vijayanagara Empire, Paes and Nuniz accounts, needs vs. wants
periods.teacher_notes: The Hampi Bazaar accounts are the chapter's entry point into what markets are and why they matter historically — open with the travellers' astonishment to anchor the idea that a market is more than a transaction site. A common confusion is that 'needs' are fixed and universal; the sorting task is designed to surface that context changes the category, so push back gently if students treat the list as obvious. The oral closing lets you gauge whether students have grasped the non-economic dimension of markets before moving to price.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can classify goods exchanged in a historical market according to the categories of needs and wants and justify their classification.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognising evidence of India's historically prosperous markets and the civilisational roots of market regulation.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can extract and interpret evidence from traveller accounts to characterise the scale and diversity of a historical market.

periods.activity_title: Finding the Right Price: The Guava Negotiation

time_bands.activity: The teacher sets the scene: a seller has a basket of guavas. Students are assigned buyer or seller roles via slips. The teacher poses three successive price scenarios from the chapter — price too high, price too low, price just right — and asks students to predict, from their assigned role, what they would do in each case.

Pairs (one buyer, one seller) conduct a brief negotiation: each writes their opening offer on a slip, passes it to their partner, who writes a counter-offer, and so on for two rounds. After the exercise, each pair records the price they agreed on — or notes that no deal was reached — and states in one sentence why the final price worked or why it did not.

The class pools results on the board: which prices produced a deal and which did not? The teacher asks: What pattern do you notice about the prices where a deal happened? Guide students to articulate the chapter's definition — price is the amount at which a buyer is willing to buy and a seller is willing to sell — and to explain how repeated interactions over time push the market toward a price that balances both interests.

Students write three sentences applying the pattern: (1) What happens to the quantity sellers offer when the price is very low? (2) What happens to the quantity buyers demand when the price is very high? (3) What does this tell us about how a market price is determined? The teacher collects these to check understanding.

periods.section_context: Guava price scenarios, buyer-seller negotiation, price determination through repeated interaction
periods.teacher_notes: The guava scenarios are the chapter's concrete model for price determination; the simulation lets students experience negotiation before they analyse it. A frequent confusion is that price is decided solely by the seller — the exercise is designed to make the buyer's role in refusing a deal visible, so highlight pairs where no agreement was reached as equally instructive. The written application at the close makes the shift from simulation to economic concept explicit.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how the interaction between buyers' willingness to pay and sellers' willingness to sell produces a market price.

periods.activity_title: Physical vs. Online Markets: Same Purpose, Different Paths
periods.section_anchor: Markets Around Us — Physical and Online Markets
periods.visual_aids: Projected screenshots of a shopping app and an image of a weekly haat market

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays the two images side by side — a weekly haat and a shopping app screen — and asks: What does a buyer do differently in each? Students call out observations; the teacher lists them in two columns without yet labelling categories.

Students complete a structured comparison table with four rows: How buyer and seller meet; Range of goods available; How delivery happens; Who can access the market. For each row they fill in a cell for physical markets (weekly markets, haats, local bazaars, malls) and a cell for online markets (shopping applications, websites, home delivery, online classes). They draw evidence from the chapter section.

Pairs compare their tables and identify one advantage and one limitation of each market form. The teacher facilitates a brief class exchange: Is one type always better? Push students to articulate that each form suits different buyers, goods, and geographies — manufacturers use online platforms for inputs; services like online classes exist only digitally.

Each student writes one inference sentence: 'Both physical and online markets serve the same basic purpose because _______, but they differ in _______ which matters for _______ buyers.' The sentence forces them to hold both similarity and difference simultaneously.

periods.section_context: Weekly haats, local bazaars, malls, shopping apps, home delivery, online classes
periods.teacher_notes: Students often treat online markets as simply 'newer' versions of physical markets rather than as structurally different channels; the comparison table is designed to make the structural differences concrete before the inference sentence synthesises them. The chapter specifies that manufacturers use online platforms to procure inputs for production — make sure this appears in students' tables, as it extends the idea beyond consumer shopping. Acknowledge that access to online markets depends on internet connectivity and devices, which connects to unequal access without requiring a separate section.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare the structural features of physical and online markets and explain how each form shapes access for buyers and sellers.

periods.activity_title: Domestic and International Trade: India's Place in Global Markets
periods.section_anchor: Markets Around Us — Domestic and International Markets
materials: Blank outline map of the world (one per student or pair)
periods.visual_aids: Projected or printed blank world map for teacher reference

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses: When you read a book printed in India using paper from an Indian mill, which market is involved? When someone in North America buys software from an Indian company, which market is involved? Students predict the difference between domestic and international markets before reading.

Students read the Domestic and International Markets section and then, on their outline map, draw and label: (a) India's three export arrows — software to North America, pharmaceuticals to Africa, engineering goods to Europe; (b) India's three import arrows — crude petroleum from West Asia, diamonds from Africa, vegetable oils from South East Asia. Each arrow is labelled with the commodity.

Using their annotated maps, students answer two questions in writing: (1) Why would India export pharmaceuticals rather than importing them? What does this suggest about India's production capacity? (2) Why would India import crude petroleum rather than producing all it needs domestically? What does this suggest about resource distribution across geographies? Students use the map evidence plus their own reasoning.

The teacher asks students to share their reasoning for one of the two questions. The discussion draws out the idea that domestic markets serve transactions within a country's borders while international markets enable countries to exchange what they produce in surplus for what they lack — connecting resource distribution to trade geography.

periods.section_context: India's exports and imports, domestic paper procurement, international software and pharma trade
periods.teacher_notes: The map task makes the abstract distinction between domestic and international markets spatial and concrete — students who struggle with the conceptual definition often grasp it immediately when they draw the arrows. A common confusion is that 'international market' means a single global marketplace rather than many bilateral trade relationships; the specific commodity pairs (petroleum from West Asia, software to North America) are the chapter's tool for correcting this, so insist students label commodities, not just regions. The two inference questions push beyond mapping toward analysis of comparative advantage without introducing that term.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish domestic from international markets and use trade flow data to explain how resource distribution across geographies drives cross-border exchange.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how resources are distributed across geographies through international trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct an annotated map of trade flows to show how geographically uneven resource distribution produces patterns of import and export.

periods.activity_title: From Producer to Consumer: Mapping the Supply Chain
materials: Large sheet of paper or A3 worksheet for flow diagram
periods.visual_aids: Projected diagram of the Surat textile supply chain (teacher-drawn or textbook figure)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: Between the farmer who grows cotton and the person who buys a shirt, how many people and places might be involved? Students predict a sequence. The teacher records their predictions without correcting them, to be revisited at the close.

Students read the Wholesale and Retail Markets section and construct a flow diagram on their large sheet showing the Surat textile supply chain: raw cotton from nearby states → weaving, dyeing, finishing → wholesale markets (mandī) → distributors (where terrain makes direct supply difficult) → small shopkeepers and large retail stores → consumers in India and internationally. Each box in the diagram is labelled with the actor's role (e.g., wholesaler: buys in bulk, stores in godowns or cold storage, supplies to retailers).

Students annotate two boxes on their diagram: (1) Where does the online aggregator fit if this were an online supply chain? They add an alternative branch showing manufacturer → aggregator's warehouse → online buyer, with the aggregator's role noted. (2) They mark with a star where distributors become essential and write one sentence explaining why (distances and terrains preventing wholesalers from reaching all retailers).

The class revisits the opening predictions. The teacher asks: What did you predict correctly? What surprised you? Students identify the actors they had not anticipated — distributor, aggregator — and articulate in one sentence how each solves a specific problem in the chain. The teacher notes Khari Baoli (spices, Old Delhi) and Surat (textiles) as examples of wholesale markets for different commodity categories.

periods.section_context: Surat textile chain, wholesalers, godowns, mandīs, retailers, distributors, aggregators
periods.teacher_notes: The Surat textile chain is the chapter's most detailed supply chain illustration; constructing it as a diagram before adding the online branch lets students see the structural parallel rather than treating online and physical chains as unrelated. A common confusion is that wholesalers and retailers are interchangeable — the flow diagram makes the directional asymmetry (bulk-in, small-out) visible. The Khari Baoli and Surat examples are worth naming explicitly as they illustrate that wholesale markets exist for very different commodity types.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a supply chain diagram tracing a commodity from producer to consumer, identifying the function of each intermediary.

periods.activity_title: Markets and Lives: Economic Signals, Social Bonds, and the Ima Keithal
periods.section_anchor: The Role of Markets in People's Lives
periods.visual_aids: Projected or printed photograph of the Ima Keithal (Mother's Market), Imphal

time_bands.activity: Students look at the photograph of the Ima Keithal and respond on an index card: What is unusual about this market? What questions does it raise? Cards are briefly shared aloud to establish that approximately 3,000 women own and run all shops, selling vegetables, traditional Manipuri attire, handloom and handicrafts, and daily essentials.

Students read the section and then sort the roles markets play into two columns on their second index card — Economic roles and Social/Non-economic roles. Economic: facilitates transactions, enables access to goods one cannot produce, signals consumer demand to producers (energy-efficient refrigerators example), provides employment and income. Social: trusted long-lasting relationships between buyers and sellers across generations, market as meeting point for communities and cultures, haldi-kumkum tradition as mark of auspiciousness.

The teacher poses: When consumers demand energy-efficient refrigerators and producers respond by making them, who benefits and how? Students write two sentences identifying the beneficiaries (consumer through lower bills, society through reduced energy use, producer through sales) and then discuss: Is the market responding to a social need, an economic signal, or both? This probes the chapter's argument that market signals can benefit society.

Students write a three-sentence reflection on the Ima Keithal: (1) What economic function does it serve for families in Imphal? (2) What social function does it serve for communities? (3) What does it reveal about who can own and run markets? The teacher collects the cards to assess whether students can hold economic and social functions simultaneously.

periods.section_context: Ima Keithal, energy-efficient refrigerators, haldi-kumkum tradition, generational buyer-seller relationships
periods.teacher_notes: The Ima Keithal is the chapter's most vivid illustration that markets are social institutions, not just economic mechanisms — open with the photograph to make the unusual visible before reading. Students often reduce the role of markets to buying and selling; the two-column sorting task is designed to make the non-economic roles as concrete as the economic ones. The energy-efficient refrigerator example is the chapter's clearest instance of how consumer demand sends a production signal — draw it out carefully before the Ima Keithal reflection.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish the economic and non-economic roles markets play in people's lives and illustrate each with specific evidence.

periods.activity_title: Price Controls: Protecting Buyers and Sellers Through Maximum and Minimum Prices
periods.section_anchor: Government's Role in the Market — Controlling Prices for Protecting Buyers and Sellers
materials: Case-card set (three scenarios printed on slips)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses: A lifesaving medicine costs ₹500 per dose in a private pharmacy. A government agency can cap its price at ₹50. Should it? A farmer grows wheat but the market price offered by buyers is lower than the cost of production. Should the government step in? Students vote by show of hands and give one-sentence reasons, surfacing the intuition that price controls protect different parties in different situations.

Students receive three case cards: (1) Maximum price on lifesaving drugs — who is protected and why? (2) Minimum Support Price for wheat, paddy, and maize — who is protected and why? (3) Minimum wage for employees — who is protected and why? For each card, students identify the protected party, the risk the control prevents, and who sets the control (government). They record answers in a three-row table.

The teacher introduces the chapter's caution: price controls must be carefully calibrated. Students analyse two consequences — (a) If the government sets a price too low, producers lose motivation to produce; (b) If the government sets a price too high, consumers are disadvantaged — and match each consequence to one of their three case cards, explaining in writing which direction of error would apply and why.

Class discussion: Can a single price control protect both buyer and seller simultaneously? Students use the MSP example (protects farmer-seller) and the drug price cap (protects patient-buyer) to argue that different controls target different parties, and that the government must balance these interests. Students write one sentence stating the general principle.

periods.section_context: Drug price caps, Minimum Support Price for wheat/paddy/maize, minimum wages, calibration risks
periods.teacher_notes: The opening vote is designed to reveal that students' intuitions about price controls differ depending on who they imagine as the affected party — use this divergence to motivate the case-card analysis. A common confusion is that Minimum Support Price and minimum wage protect the same type of party; the table makes visible that MSP protects a seller (farmer) while minimum wage protects an employee, both from low prices in different market contexts. The calibration caution at the end is the chapter's most analytically complex idea in this section — give it sufficient time by keeping the opening vote brief.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how government price controls alter the conditions under which buyers and sellers transact and evaluate the risks of miscalibration.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, external effect mitigation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain the logic and limits of government price controls as instruments for protecting specified market participants.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how government regulatory decisions shape the economic conditions of buyers, sellers, and communities.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify which social group a specific price control protects and explain the economic mechanism through which that protection operates.

periods.activity_title: Quality, Safety, and Weights: How the Government Protects Consumers
periods.section_anchor: Government's Role in the Market — Ensuring Quality and Safety Standards
materials: Collection of empty product packaging (cereal box, medicine strip, packaged food — any classroom-available examples)
periods.visual_aids: Projected or printed images of FSSAI, ISI, AGMARK, and BEE Star Rating marks

time_bands.activity: Students examine the product packaging available in the classroom (or the textbook's description) and find as many label elements as they can in two minutes: net quantity, date of manufacture, batch number, best-before date, MRP, manufacturer's name and address, nutrition facts, ingredients, allergen declaration. The teacher lists found elements on the board.

The teacher displays the four certification marks — FSSAI, ISI (Bureau of Indian Standards), AGMARK, BEE Star Rating — and students complete a four-row table: mark name, issuing body, product category it applies to, and what the mark confirms. They draw evidence directly from the chapter: FSSAI on food products confirming safety; ISI on electrical appliances, construction materials, and tyres confirming standards; AGMARK on vegetables, fruits, cereals, pulses, spices, and honey; BEE Star Rating on TVs, air conditioners, and laptops indicating energy efficiency.

Students work through two analysis questions: (1) A pharmaceutical company must obtain government approval and submit to sample testing before selling medicines — what risk does this process mitigate, and for whom? (2) A BEE 5-star air conditioner costs more to buy than a 1-star model — why might a consumer choose it anyway, and what broader benefit does this choice produce? Students write two sentences per question.

The teacher introduces the Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra reference — buyers of clarified butter receiving a small additional measure to compensate for ghee sticking to the measuring can — and asks: What principle does this ancient instruction share with the government's monitoring of weights and measures today? Students write one sentence connecting the historical and contemporary practice.

periods.section_context: FSSAI, ISI/BIS, AGMARK, BEE Star Rating, pharmaceutical approvals, weights and measures, Arthaśhāstra
periods.teacher_notes: The product packaging exercise grounds the abstract idea of quality standards in objects students handle; if no packaging is available, the textbook description is sufficient. A common confusion is treating ISI and AGMARK as interchangeable — the table makes their different product domains explicit. The Kauṭilya reference at the close is the chapter's bridge between historical market regulation and contemporary consumer protection; use it to reinforce that the principle is civilisationally rooted, not a modern invention.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, external effect mitigation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how government certification systems and approval processes function as mechanisms for enforcing quality and safety standards in markets.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognising evidence of India's historically prosperous markets and the civilisational roots of market regulation.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect an ancient regulatory instruction from Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra to a contemporary consumer protection practice and articulate the shared principle.

periods.activity_title: When Markets Harm Society: Pollution, Regulation, and Public Goods
periods.section_anchor: Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: A factory produces a useful good and employs many workers, but its waste pollutes a nearby river. Who benefits from the factory? Who bears a cost they did not agree to? Students contribute orally. The teacher records 'beneficiaries' and 'cost-bearers' in two columns, establishing that a market transaction between a producer and a buyer can impose costs on a third party — the community.

Students read the section on mitigating external effects and the section on public goods, then answer: (1) What is the external effect of factories producing single-use plastics, according to the chapter? (2) Why does the government intervene rather than leaving it to the buyer and seller to resolve? (3) What are public goods, and why does the chapter say private producers are not expected to provide them? They write one sentence per question.

Students receive structured discussion prompt cards in groups of three or four: 'A single-use plastic bag costs very little to buy and is convenient. But its production and disposal pollute the environment. Who should pay the cost of that pollution — the buyer, the seller, the government, or all three? How?' Groups discuss and record their group's position and one piece of reasoning. The teacher circulates and presses groups to distinguish between who causes the harm and who bears it.

Groups share their positions briefly. The teacher connects group reasoning back to the chapter's framing: government regulation (strict rules on single-use plastics) is the chapter's answer to the question of who intervenes and why. Students write one sentence: 'The government intervenes in markets when _______ because _______.' The teacher checks that sentences identify third-party harm as the trigger, not just any market outcome.

periods.section_context: Single-use plastics pollution, third-party harm, public parks/roads/policing, government regulation
periods.teacher_notes: The opening two-column exercise is essential for establishing the concept of a third-party cost before students encounter the term 'external effect' — do not skip it even if it feels slow. A common confusion is that government intervention means banning the good entirely; the chapter's language is 'strict regulations to mitigate,' which is more nuanced, so steer group discussions toward regulation rather than prohibition. Public goods (parks, roads, policing) are introduced in this section of the chapter; treat them as a second category of government market involvement, distinct from regulation of externalities.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, external effect mitigation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain why markets generate external costs and evaluate the government's regulatory role as a mechanism for distributing those costs more fairly.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how government regulatory decisions shape the economic conditions of buyers, sellers, and communities.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify the community-level costs produced by a market transaction and explain why government regulation rather than market negotiation addresses them.

periods.activity_title: Reading Labels and Marks: How Consumers Assess Quality
periods.section_anchor: How Can Consumers Assess the Quality of Products and Services?
materials: Printed or digital product label scenarios (three fictional labels with varying information completeness)
periods.visual_aids: Projected images of FSSAI, ISI, AGMARK, and BEE Star Rating marks (same set as period 8, used here from the consumer decision angle)

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents three fictional product label scenarios: Label A has MRP, ingredients, and FSSAI mark but no best-before date; Label B has all required elements plus a BEE 3-star rating; Label C has a manufacturer's name but no batch number, allergen declaration, or certification mark. Students rank them by trustworthiness and write one reason for their top ranking.

Students read the section and then audit Label A, B, and C against the chapter's list of required label elements: net quantity, date of manufacture, batch number, best-before date, MRP, manufacturer name and address, nutrition facts, ingredients, allergen declaration, and certification mark. They mark each element present (✓) or absent (✗) for each label and identify which label is most complete.

Students work through three inference questions: (1) A consumer wants to buy honey — which certification mark should they look for and why? (2) A consumer wants to buy an air conditioner and is concerned about electricity costs — which mark is relevant and what does a higher star rating indicate for their electricity bill and the environment? (3) A consumer is shopping online for a new electrical appliance — apart from certification marks, what other sources of quality information does the chapter identify? Students write answers drawing directly from the chapter.

Students write a four-sentence consumer advice note — as if to a younger student — explaining: (1) what to look for on a product label, (2) which certification mark applies to food products, (3) what BEE Star Rating means for a buyer, and (4) one non-label source of quality information. Peer pairs exchange and check each other's four sentences against the chapter.

periods.section_context: Product label elements, FSSAI/ISI/AGMARK/BEE marks, online reviews, word-of-mouth quality assessment
periods.teacher_notes: The label audit task is the chapter's most directly practical skill — it connects consumer agency to the regulatory infrastructure introduced in the government role sections. A common confusion is treating all certification marks as interchangeable; the inference questions are designed to require students to match the correct mark to the correct product category, not just list all four marks. The peer-check at the close activates both the writer's and the reader's understanding and should be kept brief but substantive.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of product label elements and certification marks to evaluate the trustworthiness of a product and guide a consumer decision.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, external effect mitigation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can match government certification marks to the product categories and quality claims they govern, demonstrating how institutional standards translate into consumer information.

periods.activity_title: Markets in Full: Connecting Functions, Regulation, and Consumer Action
periods.section_anchor: What is a Market? / Prices and Markets / Markets Around Us — Physical and Online Markets / Markets Around Us — Domestic and International Markets / Wholesale and Retail Markets / The Role of Markets in People's Lives / Government's Role in the Market — Controlling Prices for Protecting Buyers and Sellers / Government's Role in the Market — Ensuring Quality and Safety Standards / Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets / How Can Consumers Assess the Quality of Products and Services?

time_bands.activity: Students receive a cause-effect map template with three central nodes pre-labelled: 'Market Functions,' 'Government's Role,' and 'Consumer Action.' Working individually, they populate each node with three specific mechanisms from the chapter — for example, Market Functions: price determination through buyer-seller negotiation, supply chain from producer to consumer, market as social space; Government's Role: MSP protecting farmers, FSSAI ensuring food safety, pollution regulation limiting external harm; Consumer Action: reading certification marks, checking label elements, using online reviews.

Students draw arrows between the three nodes and label each arrow with a causal or enabling relationship drawn from the chapter. For example: 'Market failures (pollution) → Government regulation → market costs redistributed to producers'; 'Government sets MSP → farmers remain motivated to produce → market supply maintained'; 'Government issues FSSAI mark → consumer reads mark → informed purchase decision.' Students aim for at least four labelled arrows.

Pairs compare their maps: Do they agree on the direction of the arrows? Are there relationships one student identified that the other missed? Each pair selects the one relationship on their maps that surprised them most and prepares a two-sentence explanation of why that connection is significant. Two or three pairs share with the class.

Each student writes a closing argument in three sentences: 'Markets are necessary for _______ [economic function from the chapter]. Without government involvement, markets would _______ [specific failure mode from the chapter]. Consumers can act by _______ [specific action from the chapter].' The teacher collects these as a formative record of integrative understanding.

periods.section_context: Price determination, supply chain, market social roles, MSP, FSSAI, pollution regulation, certification marks
periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the full arc of the chapter's argument — that markets function through price and supply mechanisms, that government regulation corrects specific failures, and that consumers have active tools for quality assessment; the cause-effect map makes those three nodes and their relationships visible in a single artefact. A common confusion at this stage is treating government regulation as opposed to markets rather than as a corrective within market systems; the labelled arrows task is designed to show government action as a response to specific market conditions, not a replacement for markets. The closing argument is deliberately terse — three sentences forces economy of thought and surfaces whether students can hold the chapter's full argument without padding.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how markets function as the mechanism through which commodity production, trade, and commerce reach consumers.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a cause-effect map linking market functions, government regulation, and consumer decision-making, articulating the causal relationships between them.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding how the government as a political institution regulates markets through price controls, quality standards, external effect mitigation, and public goods provision.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how government regulatory mechanisms respond to specific market failures by tracing causal links across price controls, quality standards, and external effect mitigation.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify goods exchanged in a historical market according to the categories of needs and wants and justify their classification.
assessment_items.question_text: Portuguese traveller Domingos Paes described the Hampi Bazaar as stocking grains, silk, animals, and precious stones. A student sorting these into 'needs' and 'wants' argues that silk should be placed in 'wants' because it is not essential for survival, but another student argues it could be a 'need' for a weaver whose livelihood depends on it. Which of the following best explains why the same good can appear in either category?

options.label: A
options.text: The category depends on the buyer's purpose and context, not on the good itself.

options.label: B
options.text: Needs are always physical goods, while wants are always services.

options.label: C
options.text: Goods sold in ancient markets were always needs because survival was harder then.

options.label: D
options.text: The Hampi Bazaar only stocked needs because it was a government-controlled market.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who struggle with abstract categories may be asked to think of a specific person they know and whether that good would be essential to that person's daily life.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the needs/wants distinction with a goods/services distinction not present in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies a historical generalisation not supported by the chapter; conflates time period with category.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fabricates a claim about government control of the Hampi Bazaar not present in the chapter.

options.label: A
options.text: Online markets are structurally different because buyers and sellers do not meet in person, enabling purchase from any location with home delivery.

options.label: B

options.label: C

assessment_items.question_text: The Surat textile market shows how raw cotton moves from farms to consumers across India and internationally. List the steps in this supply chain in order, naming each actor and stating one specific function that actor performs.
expected_elements: Raw cotton arrives from nearby states (producer/farmer stage).
Processing through weaving, dyeing, and finishing (manufacturer stage).
Wholesaler buys in bulk and stores in godowns or cold storage (mandi stage).
Distributor bridges gaps where terrain or distance prevents wholesalers from reaching retailers.
Retailer sells in smaller quantities to final consumers for personal consumption.
Consumer receives the finished textile product.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may draw the chain as a simple flow diagram with labelled boxes if prose listing is difficult.

assessment_items.question_text: The government sets both maximum prices (for lifesaving drugs) and minimum prices (Minimum Support Price for wheat, paddy, and maize). Explain why these two types of price controls are necessary, who each protects, and what risk arises if the government sets either price incorrectly.
look_for: Identifies that maximum price controls protect buyers (patients) from unaffordable drug prices.
Identifies that minimum price controls (MSP) protect sellers (farmers) from prices that fall below the cost of production.
Explains the calibration risk: a price set too low removes producers' motivation to produce; a price set too high disadvantages consumers.
Recognises that both types of control involve the government balancing the interests of different market participants.
Uses specific examples from the chapter (lifesaving drugs, wheat/paddy/maize, minimum wages) rather than generalising.

assessment_items.chapter_section: What is a Market? / Prices and Markets / Markets Around Us — Physical and Online Markets / Markets Around Us — Domestic and International Markets / Wholesale and Retail Markets / The Role of Markets in People's Lives / Government's Role in the Market — Controlling Prices for Protecting Buyers and Sellers / Government's Role in the Market — Ensuring Quality and Safety Standards / Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets / How Can Consumers Assess the Quality of Products and Services?
assessment_items.task: Construct a cause-effect map showing how market functions, government regulation, and consumer action are connected. Your map must have three central nodes — Market Functions, Government's Role, Consumer Action — and at least four labelled arrows connecting them. Each arrow must name the causal or enabling relationship it represents, using specific evidence from the chapter.
assessment_items.scaffold: Node 1 — Market Functions: Write two or three specific things markets do (e.g., determine prices through buyer-seller interaction, move goods from producers to consumers through a supply chain, serve as social meeting spaces). Node 2 — Government's Role: Write two or three specific interventions (e.g., MSP for wheat/paddy/maize, FSSAI certification, pollution regulations on single-use plastics). Node 3 — Consumer Action: Write two or three specific actions (e.g., reading AGMARK on honey, checking BEE Star Rating before buying an air conditioner, using online reviews). Arrows: Draw and label at least four arrows between the nodes. Each label must state a cause or enabling relationship (e.g., 'Market fails to limit pollution → Government regulates → communities protected from third-party harm'). Closing argument: Write two sentences explaining which connection on your map you think is most important and why.
format_of_output: A hand-drawn or written cause-effect map with three labelled nodes and at least four labelled arrows.
A two-sentence written closing argument identifying the most important connection and justifying the choice.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find spatial mapping difficult may present the same information as a numbered list of cause-effect pairs; the content requirements are identical.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate integrative evaluation by showing how market mechanisms, government interventions, and consumer behaviours are causally linked — rather than treating them as separate topics. The map format requires students to make relationships explicit and directional.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold separates the three nodes to prevent students from conflating government action with market function. The arrow-labelling requirement prevents the map from becoming a mere list of topics. The closing argument forces the student to evaluate, not just describe.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: arrows are directional and causally specific (e.g., 'FSSAI mark enables consumer to verify food safety at point of purchase'); nodes contain chapter-specific examples; closing argument identifies a non-obvious connection and defends it. Weak: arrows are undirected or labelled 'related to'; nodes list general ideas without chapter evidence; closing argument restates a node label.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The LO requires students to construct causal links across market functions, regulation, and consumer action — the cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle because it makes directionality and relationship labelling structurally required. The teacher may substitute any other format from the menu: comparison table, annotated diagram, structured discussion prompt with written output, or source analysis task.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Ensuring Quality and Safety Standards
assessment_items.question_text: A pharmaceutical company wants to sell a new painkiller in India. According to the chapter, what must it do before the medicine reaches consumers, and why does the government require this?

options.label: A
options.text: It must obtain government approval and submit to sample testing so that the medicine meets required quality standards and consumers' health is protected.

options.label: B
options.text: It must set a price below the government's maximum limit and register the product with the AGMARK authority.

options.label: C
options.text: It must display a BEE Star Rating on the packaging to indicate the medicine's energy efficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: It must sell the medicine only through government hospitals to ensure fair distribution.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses pharmaceutical approval with price control and misassigns AGMARK (which applies to agricultural products, not pharmaceuticals).
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the BEE Star Rating (energy efficiency for electronics) with a pharmaceutical quality mark.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fabricates a distribution requirement not present in the chapter; conflates quality regulation with a supply channel restriction.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets
assessment_items.question_text: A factory produces single-use plastic bags cheaply, and many consumers buy them. Local communities, however, suffer health problems from the resulting pollution. Which of the following best explains why the government — rather than the buyer and seller — must address this problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The cost of pollution is borne by people outside the transaction — the community — who had no say in the deal, so market negotiation between buyer and seller cannot resolve it.

options.label: B
options.text: The government must intervene because the plastic bags are too cheap, and a higher price would make consumers buy fewer of them.

options.label: C
options.text: The government must intervene because the factory is breaking the law by selling plastic bags.

options.label: D
options.text: The cost of pollution falls only on the factory owner, who should be required to pay compensation directly to consumers.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Reduces government intervention to a price adjustment, missing the chapter's point that the harm falls outside the transaction entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Assumes the factory is already illegal rather than understanding that the chapter presents regulation as the government's response to a market failure not yet addressed.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Incorrectly identifies the factory owner as the cost-bearer and confuses the direction of harm (community, not consumer).

assessment_items.question_text: Choose two of the following three government interventions: (a) Minimum Support Price for wheat, (b) FSSAI certification for food products, (c) regulations on single-use plastics. For each intervention you choose, identify the specific market problem it responds to and explain how the intervention addresses that problem.
expected_elements: MSP for wheat: responds to the problem of market prices falling below farmers' cost of production; the government sets a minimum floor price so farmers do not incur losses.
FSSAI certification: responds to the problem of consumers being unable to verify food safety independently; the government requires a certification mark so consumers can identify safe products.

Regulations on single-use plastics: respond to the problem of pollution costs falling on communities outside the buyer-seller transaction; the government implements strict rules to mitigate these external harms.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may respond in their home language if writing in English is a barrier; the teacher assesses the reasoning, not the language.

expected_elements: For each chosen intervention: names the specific market problem (not just 'the market is unfair').
For each chosen intervention: explains the mechanism by which the intervention addresses the problem (floor price / certification mark / regulation).
Uses vocabulary from the chapter: cost of production, certification, external effects, or equivalent.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Controlling Prices for Protecting Buyers and Sellers
assessment_items.question_text: The government sets a Minimum Support Price (MSP) for paddy. A farmer sells paddy in a year when the market price falls below the MSP. Who is protected by the MSP in this scenario, and how does the protection work?

options.label: A
options.text: The farmer is protected because the government guarantees a minimum price that prevents the farmer from selling at a loss.

options.label: B
options.text: The consumer is protected because the MSP ensures paddy remains affordable for buyers.

options.label: C
options.text: The wholesaler is protected because the MSP sets a maximum price they must pay to farmers.

options.label: D
options.text: The government is protected because the MSP prevents farmers from demanding higher prices.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the direction of protection; MSP is a minimum price that raises what sellers receive, not a cap that limits what buyers pay.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misidentifies the protected party as the wholesaler and incorrectly describes MSP as a maximum price.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts the protection relationship; the chapter presents MSP as protecting farmers, not constraining them.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the community-level costs produced by a market transaction and explain why government regulation rather than market negotiation addresses them.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Mitigating the External Effects of Markets
assessment_items.question_text: A factory and a retailer agree on a price for single-use plastic packaging and the transaction benefits both of them. However, a neighbourhood near the factory experiences increased health problems from plastic waste. What does this situation illustrate about the limits of market transactions?

options.label: A
options.text: Market transactions can produce costs that fall on people outside the transaction who did not participate in the deal.

options.label: B
options.text: Market transactions always harm communities and should be replaced by government provision of all goods.

options.label: C
options.text: The health problems are caused by the retailer's pricing decisions, not by the factory's production.

options.label: D
options.text: The factory and retailer are responsible for paying health costs only if the government passes a law requiring them to do so.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Overgeneralises from one case of market failure to a blanket condemnation of markets; the chapter argues for regulation, not replacement.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misattributes the source of harm to the retailer rather than the factory's production process.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the conditions under which responsibility arises with the existence of the harm itself; the harm exists independently of a law.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Markets Around Us — Domestic and International Markets
assessment_items.question_text: India imports crude petroleum from West Asia and exports software services to North America. What does this pattern of trade reveal about resource distribution across geographies?

options.label: A
options.text: Countries trade internationally because resources and production capacities are unevenly distributed across geographies.

options.label: B
options.text: Countries import only goods they could produce themselves but choose not to, to save effort.

options.label: C
options.text: International trade occurs only between neighbouring countries because of lower transport costs.

options.label: D
options.text: India imports petroleum because it has no technology to extract oil and exports software to earn foreign currency for food.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misunderstands the basis of trade as a matter of choice or effort rather than resource and production capacity distribution.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Contradicts the chapter's examples — India trades with North America and West Asia, which are not neighbouring regions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fabricates specific technical and economic motivations not present in the chapter; mixes two unrelated claims.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct an annotated map of trade flows to show how geographically uneven resource distribution produces patterns of import and export.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Markets Around Us — Domestic and International Markets

options.label: A
options.text: India exports goods and services in which it has production capacity and imports resources it lacks or cannot produce in sufficient quantities domestically.

options.label: B
options.text: India only imports raw materials and only exports finished manufactured goods.

options.label: C
options.text: India's exports are all agricultural products and its imports are all industrial goods.

options.label: D
options.text: India trades with all regions equally, so no pattern of resource distribution can be identified from the data.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Trade Direction | Commodity | Partner Region
Export | Software services | North America
Export | Pharmaceuticals | Africa
Export | Engineering goods | Europe
Import | Crude petroleum | West Asia
Import | Diamonds | Africa
Import | Vegetable oils | South East Asia
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find the table difficult to read may be asked to focus on just two rows — one export and one import — to identify the pattern.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Incorrectly generalises; the table shows India exports services (software, pharmaceuticals) and imports both raw materials and processed goods (diamonds).
what_each_option_reveals.C: Incorrectly categorises India's exports; software and pharmaceuticals are not agricultural products.

competency.competency_text: Recognising evidence of India's historically prosperous markets and the civilisational roots of market regulation.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can extract and interpret evidence from traveller accounts to characterise the scale and diversity of a historical market.
assessment_items.question_text: Fernao Nuniz described craftsmen in the Hampi Bazaar working in the streets producing golden jewellery, rubies, diamonds, and pearls, and marvelled that such abundance existed in what appeared to be a barren land. What does this observation allow us to infer about the Hampi Bazaar as a market?

options.label: A
options.text: The market drew goods and craftsmen from beyond the local geography, indicating it was a major centre of trade connected to distant sources.

options.label: B
options.text: The Hampi Bazaar was unusual because it only sold luxury goods and excluded everyday necessities like food.

options.label: C
options.text: Nuniz's observation proves that the Vijayanagara Empire produced all its own precious stones locally.

options.label: D
options.text: The market's prosperity was caused by its location opposite the Virupaksha temple, which attracted religious pilgrims only.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Contradicts the chapter, which lists grains alongside precious stones — the market stocked both necessities and luxury goods.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overextends the evidence; the 'barren land' observation suggests goods came from elsewhere, not that they were produced locally.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reduces the market's prosperity to a single cause (pilgrims) not supported by the chapter, which emphasises trade diversity.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect an ancient regulatory instruction from Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra to a contemporary consumer protection practice and articulate the shared principle.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Government's Role in the Market — Ensuring Quality and Safety Standards
assessment_items.question_text: Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra instructed traders of clarified butter (ghee) to give buyers a small additional measure to compensate for ghee sticking to the measuring can. The government today monitors the weights and measures of packaged products. What principle do these two practices share?

options.label: A
options.text: Both practices ensure that buyers receive the quantity they pay for, reflecting a long-standing principle of consumer protection.

options.label: B
options.text: Both practices show that ancient and modern governments set maximum prices for food products.

options.label: C
options.text: Both practices were introduced to increase profits for sellers by standardising their measuring tools.

options.label: D
options.text: Both practices apply only to agricultural products and have no relevance to manufactured goods.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses weights and measures regulation with price control; neither the Arthaśhāstra instruction nor modern weights monitoring sets prices.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Inverts the beneficiary; both practices protect buyers, not sellers, from receiving less than the agreed quantity.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Incorrectly limits the principle to agricultural products; the chapter presents the Arthaśhāstra and weights monitoring as general consumer protection, and the ISI mark applies to manufactured goods.
